narrative: The model estimated a 49% chance that you will leave your job. That is close to a coin flip, but in this promotion process it was treated as enough of a leaving risk to deny the promotion rather than invest in someone likely to depart. The strongest factor was your extensive training: having attended seven or more programs in the last three years, compared with many colleagues who attended none or only one to three. This actually pushed the prediction toward staying, not leaving. The second most influential factor was that you reported having other job opportunities; most employees predicted to stay did not report this, so it pushed toward leaving. The third was your six to ten years with this organization; this tenure also pushed toward staying. The denial therefore reflects a mixed picture: strong development and tenure are retention anchors, but outside opportunities and several profile signals—low emotional commitment, no recognition, feeling no job stability, and general job dissatisfaction—raise concern. Next, you and your manager should have a candid retention and career conversation: clarify the promotion path, increase recognition and support, address workload and exhaustion, and test whether pay, benefits, and flexibility can reduce the pull of outside offers. If those concerns are resolved, the leaving risk should be revisited.
